newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian judges join opposition to Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Serbian judges join opposition to Milosevic.

text.p: Five supreme court judges joined swelling opposition to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Tuesday and accused their colleagues of being politically subservient to Milosevic in disputed municipal elections.

The judges published their attack in the opposition daily Nasa Borba as 10,000 students began a 16th straight day of Belgrade demonstrations against Milosevic, buoyed by open support from the United States, France and Britain.
Washington warned Milosevic it would be "outraged" if he used police to crush the demonstrations which have regularly grown to as many as 100,000 people.
The State Department called the elections "a sham" after Milosevic denied the Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties of victories in the capital and other cities.
The judge's revolt was the first sign of a crack in the machinery of state over which Milosevic has maintained a tight grip during nine years of authoritarian government.
Judge Zoran Ivosevic accused some of the 36 supreme court judges of being politically subservient and wrote:
"The Serbian supreme court has unfortunately not had the strength and the courage to give the electorate what belongs to it on the basis of the election results."
Serbian courts rubber-stamped socialist claims of unspecified "irregularities" in the elections to clear the way for fresh elections which the socialists claimed they won.

A second protest letter, signed by Ivosevic and four judges belonging to the court, referred to the opposition claim of election robbery and said the legal profession should not be associated with theft.
The authorities, who have refrained from using police intervention so far, stepped up a media campaign against the opposition. State-run newspapers branded Zajedno as "terrorist".
The opposition "wants to seize power by force" and its protests "concealed terrorism", wrote Vecernje Novosti, a mouthpiece for the socialist Party.
The harsh attacks were interpreted as a warning from Milosevic that he would not tolerate street protests indefinitely.
With no sign of the demonstrations flagging and international criticism growing, Milosevic was looking for a way out of the crisis to save face, diplomats said.
The government cancelled a parliament session for Tuesday when the Zajedno coalition had planned to stage its biggest protest yet to demand the alleged poll fraud be overturned.
Authorities, gambling the demonstrations would eventually fizzle out, cancelled the session to avoid possible clashes while the international spotlight was fixed on Belgrade.
The United States warned Milosevic that his refusal to recognise the result of the elections strengthened its resolve to keep remaining U.N. sanctions against Belgrade.
These deny Serbia access to foreign credits it needs urgently to rebuild its economy.
Although anxious to get all sanctions removed, Milosevic has shown a willingness in the past to ignore international condemnation to maintain his grip on power.

Opposition leaders said they still lacked crucial support from trades unions which have held back from the demonstrations although some workers joined protests in industrial centres such as the southern town of Nis.
